dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — and a big welcome to Benji, who arrived this weekend after Saturday night's hospital trip. It is a cloudy, mild Monday in Solon, high near 64°, with no rain expected and the first early sunset of standard time at 5:19 tonight. Overnight, Iran left the Doha talks with a draft U.S. deal circulating that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the naval blockade ends, while Senator Chris Murphy was hospitalized after a stroke at his son's hockey game, with a full recovery expected. There is no early voting today, so tomorrow is the day: polls are open 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM for the midterms, and 66 Cuyahoga County precincts — including some in Solon — have new polling places, so check yours before you go. Tonight's home entertainment is set too, with the Cavs hosting Oklahoma City at Rocket Arena at 7 PM.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
Iran leaves the Doha talks with a draft deal circulating — reopening Hormuz still hinges on ending the U.S. blockade
items.summary:
Iran's negotiators have left their talks with Qatari mediators in Doha, and a draft proposal for a deal with the United States is now being circulated, an official briefed on the discussions said Monday. The Iranian team departed on Sunday, and the official stressed the departure was not caused by any breakdown in the talks, with a follow-up meeting possible.

The framework on the table is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the American naval blockade of Iran. Tehran now says the plan could move faster than first proposed — Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has floated reopening the strait in about two days under a deal, down from a week. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei confirmed Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi had been in Doha exchanging messages with Washington through the Qataris; there are still no direct U.S.-Iran talks.

Baghaei also set Tehran's red line in plain terms: no final agreement starts, and the strait does not reopen, unless the blockade ends and Iran's demands are respected. President Trump rejected Iran's first version of the proposal, and while he has said the U.S. will not launch new attacks before Tuesday's midterms and calls the talks productive, he has not ruled out more military action afterward.

Watch for news of a follow-up meeting in Doha, and for the first market reaction — Gulf stocks were already moving on the headlines Monday, with Qatar's benchmark index up 2.2 percent.

items.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of using the Kherson ceasefire to reinforce — as strikes cut power to hundreds of thousands
items.summary:
Ukraine's military said Monday that Russia used last week's six-day local ceasefire around Oleshky in the Kherson region to rotate troops, strengthen positions, expand anti-drone defenses and stockpile ammunition. The pause, the longest local truce since the full-scale invasion began in 2022, expired Sunday evening, and Ukraine says the quiet was used to prepare for more fighting rather than to step back from it.

The ceasefire had a real humanitarian result while it lasted: about 180 people, including 23 children, were evacuated from the area around Oleshky on the occupied bank of the Dnipro River. It was brokered with the involvement of First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov responded that Moscow assumes Ukraine also regrouped during the pause, calling it normal practice, and said no similar ceasefires are planned.

The wider war did not pause at all. Russian strikes on power infrastructure in four regions left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian households without electricity over the weekend — Ukraine says it shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched since Saturday evening — while Ukrainian drones caused significant damage to an industrial facility in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, home to a major refinery. Russian shelling and drone attacks hit 16 settlements in the Kherson region in the day to Monday morning.

With winter approaching, both sides are treating energy as a central front. Watch whether Ukraine's power cuts harden into rolling blackouts, and whether fuel supplies in the affected Russian regions stay tight.

items.title: Nearly a billion barrels of oil have drained from global stockpiles since Hormuz was disrupted, ADNOC's chief says
items.summary:
The head of Abu Dhabi's national oil company, Sultan Al Jaber, said Monday that nearly a billion barrels of oil have been drawn out of global inventories since shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. That is the world's emergency cushion being steadily used up.

Inventories are what stand between a supply shock and a price shock. While tankers sit idle and flows through the strait run at a fraction of normal, refiners and governments have been meeting demand by pulling oil out of storage instead. That works until it doesn't — every month of drawdown leaves the system with less ability to absorb the next surprise.

The warning landed the same weekend OPEC+ kept its December production targets steady, with oil holding near $120 a barrel and producers openly uncertain about quotas for 2027. It also explains why Monday's hints of progress in the Doha talks pulled oil prices down more than 4 percent in early trading: traders are pricing the stockpile math, not just the diplomacy.

Watch the next round of weekly inventory reports. If draws continue at this pace while Hormuz stays restricted, pressure for a deal — or for emergency releases — builds quickly.

items.title: Spain has identified 66 of the 69 people killed in last week's high-speed train crash, including four Americans
items.summary:
Spanish authorities said Monday that 66 of the 69 people killed in Wednesday's high-speed train collision near Urda, in Toledo province south of Madrid, have now been formally identified. Fifty-four of the dead are Spanish citizens and 12 are foreign nationals, identified through fingerprints and DNA testing.

The confirmed foreign dead include four Americans, along with citizens of Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia, the Czech Republic, France and Portugal. Three missing-person reports remain open — two Australians and one Japanese citizen — and the three still-unidentified victims are believed to be foreign nationals. Thirty-nine people remain in hospital, nine of them in intensive care.

The crash happened when a state Renfe train struck the back of a stationary private Iryo train on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed line. Early findings describe the Renfe train traveling at 100 to 125 mph and a control center authorizing it to proceed after a safety-system failure had halted traffic on the stretch — an order the transport minister has called inexplicable, though no final cause has been established.

The line remains closed, ticket sales on the route are suspended into December, and the transport minister faces parliament on Tuesday. It is Spain's deadliest rail accident since 2013, and its second fatal high-speed collision this year.

items.title: No winner in Israel: Netanyahu's bloc stalls at 53 seats, and Arab parties hold the balance of power
items.summary:
A week after Israel's election, neither side has the 61 seats needed to govern the 120-seat Knesset. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud is the largest single party with 27 seats, but his bloc of right-wing and ultra-Orthodox allies totals 53 — well down from the 68-seat majority he held before the vote.

Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party won 21 seats and his bloc 48. The decisive numbers belong to the Arab parties, which won a record 19 seats combined. Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett said Sunday his party will recommend Eisenkot to President Isaac Herzog to form the government, and senior Arab party officials are reported to be leaning the same way, which could give Eisenkot the first chance at building a coalition.

Herzog's formal consultations begin Wednesday, and whoever gets the mandate has 28 days, plus a possible two-week extension, to assemble a government. Herzog has publicly urged the factions to stop posturing and negotiate, warning against dragging the country into yet another election. Eisenkot has set conditions for partners, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and universal military or civilian service, and his bloc has ruled out a unity government with Netanyahu.

Watch Wednesday's consultations. If Eisenkot gets the mandate, Israel's next government could depend on Arab parties in a way it never has before.

items.title: Nearly a million New Zealanders have already voted — early turnout is up 28% ahead of Saturday's election
items.summary:
New Zealand's Electoral Commission said Monday that 913,762 votes were cast in the first week of early voting for the country's general election — nearly a million ballots, and 28 percent more than in the same period in 2023. Saturday alone saw more than 190,000 votes issued.

About 600 voting places are open each day this week, rising to more than 2,300 on election day, which is Saturday, November 7. Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne called the start strong, with six more days of voting still to go.

The surge comes despite controversy over new government rules that closed voter enrolment 13 days before the election — critics argued the earlier cutoff would suppress participation. So far, the turnout numbers point the other way, though a big early vote also means many ballots are locked in before the campaign's final week.

Polls still show no clear winner or obvious coalition combination, so New Zealand could be headed for the same kind of post-election negotiation Israel is now living through. Watch the final polls and Saturday's count.

items.title: Election eve guide: Democrats need four seats in each chamber, and the Senate runs through red states
items.summary:
Americans vote Tuesday in midterms that will decide control of Congress for the final two years of President Trump's term — the first nationwide verdict on his presidency. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers, 218 to 214 in the House and 53 to 47 in the Senate, and Democrats need a net gain of four seats in each chamber to take control.

The House is widely expected to flip. The Senate is the real fight: it hinges on six to eight races, and Democrats have to win Republican-held seats in states Trump carried by double digits in 2024, including Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas. Early results from Republican-held House districts in Florida and Virginia on Tuesday night will be the first clues to the size of any Democratic gains.

Reuters identifies the two frustrations driving voters as the cost of living and the war with Iran. A Democratic win in either chamber would likely bring investigations into the administration, immigration enforcement and the war — which is why the White House has spent months preparing to govern by executive action if it loses Congress.

The first polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday. Watch those early Florida and Virginia House results, and expect some close Senate races to stay unresolved into Wednesday.

items.title: The Justice Department is intervening in Tuesday's election in ways it has avoided for decades — and courts keep pushing back
items.summary:
President Trump's Justice Department has intervened directly in the midterm elections, breaking with a decades-long practice of keeping law enforcement visibly separate from contests it could appear to influence. In California, the department sought to set aside mail ballots from about 20,000 voters it says are likely noncitizens, and demanded records in a related criminal investigation. In Alaska, it sued to block certification of the Senate result if the Republican incumbent loses narrowly.

The courts have not gone along. Judges have rejected the department's suits in both states, and on Sunday a federal judge in Anchorage dismissed the Alaska case, finding the state could not conduct the kind of investigation the department wanted while preserving the secrecy of the ballot. The department has appealed the Alaska ruling.

Attorney General Todd Blanche says the efforts are lawful and aimed at protecting the integrity of the vote, insisting the department is enforcing the law rather than helping any campaign. Critics argue the moves lay groundwork for challenging results the administration dislikes. Election administration in the United States belongs to the states, and state audits and independent studies have consistently found voter fraud to be rare.

Watch for any emergency appeal before Tuesday, and for how the department's roughly 1,000 planned election monitors are received in the counties where they deploy.

items.title: Netanyahu pressed Trump to strike Iran right after the midterms — Trump wants to give talks more time
items.summary:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed President Trump in a phone call on Saturday to launch fresh military strikes on Iran immediately after Tuesday's midterm elections, according to Axios, citing one U.S. and one Israeli official. One Israeli source described the call as tough; an American source called it direct. Trump, asked about it in Iowa on Sunday, called it a very good talk and confirmed Iran was discussed, without giving details.

Trump's public position is that he is in no hurry. He has told reporters negotiations with Iran are going fine, has told Congress he does not intend to strike before the midterms, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday no decision on new strikes has been made and the president would prefer a diplomatic resolution. Neither the White House nor Netanyahu's office commented on the report.

Behind the diplomacy, the military track is still moving: the U.S. and Israel have reportedly drawn up a plan for a new operation that could be activated right after the election if talks break down. Vice President JD Vance also sent a letter last week to a senior Iranian security official about restarting formal negotiations — the highest-level American outreach to Tehran in months — and Iran's answer restated its conditions, including unfreezing assets, ending the naval blockade and lifting sanctions.

That makes election week a fork in the road: a draft deal is circulating in Doha while a strike plan sits ready. Watch which track moves first once the votes are counted.

items.title: Trump closes the campaign in Iowa and Kansas: 'We have to get the Senate'
items.summary:
President Trump closed the final weekend of the midterm campaign with rallies in Dubuque, Iowa, and Salina, Kansas on Sunday — two states he has won comfortably before, where Republicans are now defending Senate seats they cannot afford to lose. He reversed an earlier decision to cancel both stops in favor of tele-rallies.

On Air Force One he put the stakes in one sentence: 'We have to get the Senate.' In Iowa he boosted Senate candidate Ashley Hinson in a speech of about two hours, flanked by House Speaker Mike Johnson and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. In Kansas, after an Air Force One flyover at Salina's airport, he campaigned for Senator Roger Marshall's re-election alongside Secretary of State Marco Rubio, telling the crowd it was the last stop of the cycle. Since October 1, Trump has held more than two dozen rallies in 19 states.

The rallies were aimed at a shrinking target: more than 54 million votes had already been cast before the final weekend, so closing events are about turning out supporters who still vote in person on Election Day itself. Trump also used the stops to praise Michigan Representative Haley Stevens for endorsing a Republican Senate candidate and to attack Democratic nominees in Kansas and Michigan.

One stop remains: a closing pitch at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington on Monday, the last full day of the campaign.

items.title: Sen. Chris Murphy is hospitalized after a stroke at his son's hockey game — a full recovery is expected
items.summary:
Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut, 53, suffered a stroke on Saturday while attending his son's hockey game, his office announced Sunday. He noticed numbness in his arm during the game, was taken to a local hospital where doctors confirmed a stroke, and was then transferred to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore for further monitoring.

His chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said doctors are encouraged by his progress, that he is awake and alert and responding well to treatment, and that his team is optimistic he will make a full recovery. No type of stroke and no timetable for his discharge or return to the Senate has been announced.

Murphy has served in the Senate since 2013 and is one of the Democrats' leading voices on gun safety and immigration. He is not on the ballot Tuesday. He had been scheduled to campaign in New Hampshire on Sunday for Representative Chris Pappas. Well wishes crossed party and chamber lines — President Trump said he was surprised and would consider reaching out, and Senator John Fetterman, who had a stroke during his own 2022 campaign, wished him a full and speedy recovery. Three other Senate Democrats have had strokes in recent years and recovered.

Days earlier, Murphy had publicly criticized a reported Pentagon plan to restart the Iran war after Election Day, following a classified briefing — a reminder of how central he has been to the Democrats' foreign-policy argument this cycle.

items.title: Two days before the vote, a Democratic congresswoman endorses the Republican in Michigan's Senate race
items.summary:
Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for the U.S. Senate on Sunday, less than 48 hours before Election Day, after losing the Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed by about a point in August. She announced it in a video after attending a Detroit church service with Rogers, saying the Democratic nominee had told her she was no longer welcome in his campaign — and that he was right, because she does not belong in it.

The break was weeks in the making. Stevens had been uninvited from a joint unity event with El-Sayed the same day, had demanded he condemn an outside group's ad, and as recently as Friday had reaffirmed she would vote for him. She called herself a very proud Democrat while breaking with her party's nominee. Her fiancé had already said he would vote for Rogers.

The reaction inside her party was immediate: Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called the endorsement a betrayal, party officials moved against her standing, and her longtime chief of staff resigned. President Trump praised the move and urged her to switch parties. Polling averages had El-Sayed ahead by roughly four points before the endorsement.

Michigan's open Senate seat is one of the races that could decide control of the chamber, and no Republican has won it since 1994. Watch whether a one-point primary loser's endorsement moves any late voters — or mainly dominates one news cycle.

items.title: Stocks bounce Monday after the AI selloff, with Apple earnings and the midterms ahead
items.summary:
Wall Street steadied on Monday morning after a brutal October for technology stocks. In early futures trading the Dow was up about 0.5 percent, the S&P 500 about 0.5 percent and the Nasdaq 100 about 0.9 percent, as most big technology names rose in premarket trading and investors took a breath.

The bounce follows a month in which the Nasdaq 100 lost more than $2.5 trillion in market value and flirted with correction territory, as investors soured on the scale of AI spending relative to the returns so far. Several companies have tapped the bond market to finance AI investment, which has sharpened the question of how that debt gets justified if borrowing costs rise. Intel, which suffered its worst one-day fall since the 1980s on Friday, inched slightly higher Monday.

The week's calendar is dense: Apple reports earnings after Monday's close, AMD follows later in the week, voters decide control of Congress on Tuesday, and the October jobs report lands Friday. Oil gave the market a tailwind, falling more than 4 percent as the Doha talks raised hopes the Iran war — and its supply disruption — could ease.

Analysts note divided government has historically been fine for markets. Watch Apple's numbers tonight for the first real test of whether the selloff was a pause or a turning point.

items.title: Apple's new CEO faces his first earnings call tonight — the holiday outlook is the real test
items.summary:
John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September, hosts his first earnings call as Apple's chief executive on Monday after the market close. Analysts expect September-quarter revenue of about $113.4 billion, up nearly 11 percent, with iPhone sales up about 15 percent to roughly $56.5 billion — though profit growth is expected to be the weakest in six quarters, squeezed by surging memory-chip costs.

The quarter itself only captures nine days of iPhone 18 Pro sales, so the numbers matter less than the guidance. Ternus's first months have been busy: Apple's first foldable phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo, went on sale October 23, alongside a smart-home hub and the first touchscreen laptops — all of which sell into the holiday quarter he is about to forecast.

The foldable is under a microscope. Some buyers have reported cracks and lines along the inner display's fold, prompting replacements, while delivery waits average about 79 days, which suggests demand is still running well ahead of supply. Cook once called rising memory costs a '100-year flood,' and Ternus will be pressed on margins, on Apple's AI plans and revamped Siri, and on the holiday outlook.

Apple's refusal to join the AI spending race has helped its stock rise about 27 percent this year, ahead of its big-tech peers. Tonight's call shows whether that discipline still looks like wisdom after the October selloff.

items.title: OpenAI wants to call its data centers 'AI compute campuses' in a post-midterm push
items.summary:
OpenAI is preparing a policy and public-relations push to begin right after Tuesday's midterms, Axios reported, including a proposal to call its largest facilities 'AI compute campuses' instead of data centers. The plans have been assembled since August and would roll out during the lame-duck session of Congress that opens November 9.

The package is broader than a name. Global affairs chief Chris Lehane described mandatory safeguards for the most powerful systems — he calls them speed limits — along with help for workers and small businesses and community agreements that give local residents a say in how projects are built. Lehane said the midterms are a preview of 2028, when he expects artificial intelligence to be the central issue in American politics.

Data centers have become one of the most contested local issues in the country, with about $173 million of mostly negative advertising mentioning them in this election cycle. Communities are fighting over power, water and land, and a name change alone settles none of that — which Lehane seemed to acknowledge, saying communities should hold companies accountable for real benefits.

Watch for the first concrete proposals after November 9, and whether rival companies adopt the 'campus' language or keep their distance.

items.title: OpenAI cuts its fundraising target to $20 billion as big investors cool on AI
items.summary:
OpenAI has cut the funding round it is trying to close from about $30 billion to $20 billion, and lowered the valuation it is seeking from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion, according to Financial Times reporting. Some large investors trimmed their commitments ahead of Friday's deadline, and the first close is now expected to come in below even the reduced target.

About $11 billion had been secured as of last week. Investors from the United Arab Emirates, including the state-backed fund MGX, are expected to provide the largest share, alongside firms such as Coatue, Founders Fund, Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz. The company now plans to top up the round from family offices and wealthy individuals in the coming weeks. OpenAI has not commented on the figures.

The cut landed in the middle of an AI selloff, with the Nasdaq 100 down about 3.5 percent on Friday, and while OpenAI's rival Anthropic is preparing its own market debut and competing for the same investor money. OpenAI's spending commitments for computing power keep growing even as the price investors will pay for a piece of it comes down.

Watch the final close figure when it is announced. In the current mood, investors will read it as a verdict on how much of the AI buildout they are still willing to fund.

items.title: AI stocks slid in October — the question now is whether the other 70% of the market can carry on without them
items.summary:
October delivered an unusual split in the U.S. stock market. The S&P 500's technology sector fell 6.8 percent, its worst month since March 2025, with the sector down 4.2 percent on Friday alone after disappointing results from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel. Yet nine of the index's eleven sectors rose in October, and more than 70 percent of S&P 500 companies ended the month higher, leaving the benchmark down less than 1 percent.

That broadening is what investors have said they wanted for two years: a market that does not live and die by a handful of AI names. The catch is size — technology is about 38 percent of the S&P 500's weight, so a deeper AI slide would be hard for the rest of the market to absorb, and the index is still up more than 10 percent this year largely because of those same stocks.

The economic entanglement runs deeper than share prices. Oxford Economics estimates about a third of recent U.S. growth stems from AI, counting both the direct infrastructure buildout and the consumer spending powered by stock gains. Hyperscaler capital spending is expected to reach about $800 billion this year and $1.2 trillion in 2027, which is why the signal investors fear most is any of them pulling back.

Watch the next round of spending guidance. If the big builders hold their plans while earnings elsewhere keep growing, October may read as a healthy rotation rather than the start of something worse.

items.title: Intel fell 29% on Friday — its worst day since 1974 — on a weak outlook and a deepening PC slump
items.summary:
Intel's shares fell nearly 29 percent on Friday, closing at $65.76 from $92.07 the day before — the company's worst single session since July 1974 and roughly $140 billion of market value gone in a day. The stock inched up about 0.2 percent in Monday premarket trading.

The trigger was guidance, not the quarter just reported. Intel's third-quarter revenue rose 21 percent to $16.5 billion and beat expectations, but it forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion against the $17.1 billion analysts expected, with margins dropping sharply. Finance chief David Zinsner blamed a deepening PC downturn he expects to last at least through the first half of next year, and said Intel is unlikely to generate positive free cash flow this year. Client computing revenue fell 5 percent in the quarter and processor shipments dropped 14 percent.

Guidance also reflects an explosion earlier in October at Intel's Kiryat Gat plant in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third; the company says the blast will reduce revenue by about $600 million across two quarters. The selling spread across the chip sector on Friday, with Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom and others down between 4 and 12 percent.

One unusual shareholder took a paper loss of roughly $12 billion on the day: the U.S. government, which holds about 10 percent of Intel from a stake acquired last year. Several banks downgraded the stock to neutral over the weekend.

items.title: A judge throws out the Justice Department's lawsuit over Alaska's two Dan Sullivans on the ballot
items.summary:
A federal judge in Anchorage dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit over Alaska's Senate ballot on Sunday, and the department immediately appealed. The suit had asked the court to prevent Alaska from certifying its Senate result if Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan loses by fewer votes than were cast for another candidate on the ballot named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

The second Sullivan is a retired schoolteacher from the fishing community of Petersburg, running with no party affiliation. Alaska's own courts had already allowed both names on the ballot after a back-and-forth in state court this summer. Reporting by The New York Times said Democratic challenger Mary Peltola's campaign had worked with an operative to find another Sullivan to run; her campaign denies involvement, and Daniel Sullivan denies running at anyone's direction.

Judge Sharon Gleason ruled the federal court lacks authority to order Alaskans' ballots segregated so federal investigators can examine them, saying that would violate voters' right to a secret ballot, and found the government lacked standing. Civil-liberties and voting groups had intervened on Alaska's side, and Senator Sullivan said Sunday he will accept the election results.

The race itself is a toss-up in Alaska's ranked-choice system, with tabulation likely on November 18 if no one wins a majority of first choices. The ruling removes one legal cloud over it, pending the appeal.

items.title: A Learjet crashes into a South Florida neighborhood, killing all nine people aboard
items.summary:
All nine people aboard a Learjet 60 were killed Sunday when the business jet crashed shortly before 1 p.m. near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North in Palm Beach County, Florida, in an area between Greenacres and Palm Springs. The jet erupted in flames, sparked several fires, scattered debris widely and left a crater beside the road. No one on the ground was reported killed or injured.

The flight had left Austin, Texas, bound for North Eleuthera in the Bahamas. Recorded radio traffic captured the crew reporting icing and moderate turbulence, then a mayday as the jet began descending at 10,000 feet per minute, then faster — flight-tracking data showed a descent rate at one point above 32,000 feet per minute, and the crew's final transmission came about 35 seconds after the first distress call. Weather near West Palm Beach at the time was overcast with rain, lightning and gusty winds.

About 600 people needed shelter or evacuation because the damage blocked the entrance to a mobile home park, and the Red Cross was placed on standby as residents were moved to county shelters. All lanes of Military Trail in the area are closed, and a county commissioner said the crater means the road is unlikely to reopen for at least 30 days. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called it a horrific tragedy, and Governor Ron DeSantis said it looked like a missile going down.

The FAA and NTSB are investigating, with the NTSB leading and a briefing expected in West Palm Beach on Monday. It is the second-deadliest U.S. plane crash this year. The cause is not yet known.

items.title: Health insurance open enrollment is open — and premiums are higher again this year
items.summary:
Open enrollment for Affordable Care Act marketplace coverage began November 1 and runs through January 15 in most states, with a December 15 deadline for coverage that starts January 1. Shoppers this year will generally find more expensive coverage, as the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits and changes in last year's reconciliation law work through the system.

Insurers have proposed raising median gross premiums by about 15 percent for 2027, attributing roughly 10 points of that to rising medical costs and about 4 points to the knock-on effects of the expired credit enhancements. There is a nuance worth knowing: because the underlying credit formula is not changing this year, the credits themselves grow with premiums, so many enrollees' actual monthly bills have not risen as sharply as the headline prices suggest.

The market has already shrunk. Between February 2025 and February 2026, marketplace enrollment fell by nearly 3 million people, about 13 percent, with some states losing close to a third of their enrollment. Analysts warn that higher prices will also push more people toward limited-benefit plans that cover far less.

The practical step is unglamorous: go to HealthCare.gov or your state marketplace, compare plans and check what financial help you qualify for, because individual situations vary widely and last year's plan may no longer be the best value.
items.source: Center on Budget and Policy Priorities

items.title: Election-eve weather: warm in the East, severe storms in the Plains, heavy snow in the Rockies
items.summary:
November is starting warm across most of the country. Temperatures on Monday run 10 to 20 degrees above average from Texas to Minnesota, and the warmth spreads east on Tuesday into the Ohio Valley, the Great Lakes and the Northeast — Indianapolis, for example, warms well into the 70s on Election Day.

A cold front moving from the central states toward the East brings the week's risks with it. About 48 million people across at least 17 states face a risk of excessive rainfall and flash flooding on Monday into early Tuesday, and more than 21 million face a risk of severe thunderstorms, mainly damaging winds and large hail with a few tornadoes possible, concentrated in states including Texas, Missouri and Kansas.

In the West, the weather is wintry. A winter storm warning covers southwest Colorado until noon Monday, with 12 to 18 inches of snow expected above 10,000 feet and gusts to 45 mph, and advisories cover high-elevation routes in Utah and Colorado through Monday, including the Eisenhower Tunnel and Berthoud Pass corridors. Moisture from a former tropical storm near Hawaii is also feeding flood risk in the Southwest.

For Tuesday's voting, forecasters expect manageable conditions in most of the East, with rain in parts of the Midwest — Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, Wisconsin, Minnesota and Michigan — the main weather factor in turnout.

items.title: A Swede wins the New York City Marathon in his first-ever marathon, in a record field of 60,000
items.summary:
Sweden's Andreas Almgren won the men's New York City Marathon on Sunday in 2 hours, 6 minutes and 1 second — in the first marathon of his career. He pulled away late to beat Italy's Yemaneberhan Crippa by 13 seconds, becoming the first Swede to win the race, the first debut winner since 2010, and the first European man to win in three decades.

Kenya's Sheila Chepkirui won the women's race in 2:24:36, reclaiming a title she first won in 2024, by pulling away from defending champion Hellen Obiri in the final stretch. American Jess McClain finished second, six seconds behind, passing Obiri in the final strides — the first American on the New York podium, men's or women's, since 2018.

Nearly 60,000 runners from more than 140 countries took part, the largest field in the race's history, in the 50th running of the five-borough course that began in 1976. Switzerland's Marcel Hug won his eighth men's wheelchair title, by a single second, and 46-year-old Edna Kiplagat, the 2010 champion, finished fourth in the women's race.

New York was the final World Marathon Major of 2026, and Almgren collected $100,000 for the win — a remarkable result for a 31-year-old world half-marathon champion whose career has repeatedly been interrupted by injuries.

items.title: Cavs host the short-handed Thunder tonight at Rocket Arena, looking for consistency
items.summary:
The Cavaliers host the Oklahoma City Thunder tonight, Monday, at 7 p.m. at Rocket Arena, with both teams sitting at 4-2. It is the first of two meetings between the teams this week, with a rematch in Oklahoma City in a few days.

Cleveland arrives off its best win of the young season: a 136-111 rout at Milwaukee on Saturday night, built on a 48-point second quarter that turned a one-point deficit into a 72-46 halftime lead. Evan Mobley scored a season-high 27 points and Jarrett Allen added 25 points and 11 rebounds — 52 combined from the frontcourt — with Donovan Mitchell scoring 15 and James Harden 13 with 7 assists. It was the Cavs' first road win of the season, and they are unbeaten in three home games.

Oklahoma City is talented but thinned out. The Thunder started 4-0, then lost two straight, including 119-98 at Houston on Saturday despite 26 points from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Chet Holmgren is out with a knee injury until around the new year, Jalen Williams is out with a serious leg injury, and Alex Caruso and Cason Wallace are also unavailable. Cleveland has its own absences — Jaylon Tyson and Nae'Qwan Tomlin are out, and Peyton Watson is questionable — and previews still made the Cavs modest favorites at home.

For a team that has alternated sharp wins with flat losses, tonight is a measuring stick: a defending-power opponent, at home, missing its second and third options. A win would make it five of six since the opening loss in Philadelphia.

items.title: Browns get sacked eight times and never reach the end zone in a 27-6 loss at Pittsburgh
items.summary:
The Steelers beat the Browns 27-6 on Sunday at Acrisure Stadium, in a game both teams entered at 5-2 with sole possession of first place in the AFC North on the line. Pittsburgh leaves at 6-2 and alone in first; Cleveland falls to 5-3 and third in the division, behind Cincinnati. The Browns' only points were Andre Szmyt field goals from 32 and 49 yards.

The game was lost in the trenches and in the first minutes. Cleveland lost fumbles on its first two drives, rushed for only 34 yards all day, and gave up eight sacks. Deshaun Watson finished 27 of 39 for 324 yards with no touchdowns, much of it after the game was decided, and lost a fumble. Pittsburgh ran 33 times for 200 yards and scored all three of its touchdowns on the ground, with Jaylen Warren carrying 17 times for 143 yards and a score. Cleveland went 0-for-3 in the red zone, including failing from the 1-yard line at the end.

It was Cleveland's 23rd straight regular-season loss in Pittsburgh, tying the NFL record for consecutive road losses to one opponent, and it means the Browns have not swept the Steelers since 1998 after winning the first meeting in October. The bright spot was tight end Harold Fannin Jr., who caught 10 passes for 154 yards.

Next up is a trip to New Orleans on Sunday, November 8, at 1 p.m., against a Saints team coming off its bye. Head coach Todd Monken's postgame verdict was blunt: the Browns earned the result, and they did not play well enough.

items.title: Ohio State kicks field goals instead of scoring touchdowns, and loses 30-18 at USC
items.summary:
No. 2 Ohio State lost 30-18 to USC on Saturday night at the Los Angeles Coliseum, dropping to 6-2 overall and 4-1 in the Big Ten while USC improved to 7-2. True freshman Luke Fahey made his first career start at quarterback with Julian Sayin injured, and he played clean football: 260 yards, one touchdown and no turnovers.

The strange part is that Ohio State dominated the stat sheet and lost anyway. The Buckeyes outgained USC 464 yards to 338 and held the ball nearly 20 minutes longer, rushed for 204 yards behind Bo Jackson's 121 — and scored only one touchdown, settling for four field goals from Connor Hawkins, who led the team with 12 points. USC scored on its second snap, a 69-yard catch-and-run, led 20-9 at halftime, and never trailed.

Self-inflicted wounds did the rest: 11 penalties, Ohio State's most since 2022, red-zone failures, dropped passes and a 44-yard punt return that set up a USC touchdown. Jeremiah Smith's touchdown catch late in the game was the 40th of his career, a Big Ten record, but the two-point try failed and USC recovered the onside kick.

Ohio State is now a two-loss team that likely has to win out, starting Saturday at home against Oregon at 3:30 p.m. Coach Ryan Day's defense of his freshman quarterback was pointed: the team around him did not play well enough to support a first road start.

items.title: Check your polling place: 66 Cuyahoga County precincts have moved for Tuesday's election, including in Solon
items.summary:
Election Day is Tuesday, November 3, and Ohio polls are open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. The Cuyahoga County Board of Elections has announced 66 precinct polling-location changes across nine cities, affecting nearly 60,000 voters — and Solon is explicitly on the list of affected cities.

Most of the Cleveland changes were forced by the Cleveland Metropolitan School District closing ten buildings that had served as polling places. The Board mailed change letters to every affected voter, and it urges everyone to confirm their location before Tuesday at boe.cuyahogacounty.gov or by calling 216-443-VOTE, because on Election Day you must vote at your assigned polling place.

Two timing rules matter this year. Early in-person voting ended Sunday at 5 p.m. — there is no early voting today, Monday. And under a state law signed last December, mail ballots must now arrive by the close of polls at 7:30 p.m. Tuesday to be counted; the old multi-day grace period is gone, so election officials say it is too late to mail a ballot and it should be dropped off in person at the Board of Elections, 1803 Superior Avenue in Cleveland.

Turnout has been strong: Cuyahoga County's early in-person vote passed 30,000 in the final week — already far beyond the entire 2022 midterm total — and the county's director projected it could exceed 40,000. Locally, county issues on the ballot include levies for developmental disabilities services and for health and human services.

items.title: Ohio picks a governor and a senator tomorrow — and both races are down to the wire
items.summary:
Ohio voters will choose a governor and a U.S. senator on Tuesday, on a ballot that also decides other statewide offices. Democrat Amy Acton, running with David Pepper, faces Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, running with Robert McColley, to succeed term-limited Governor Mike DeWine. In the Senate race, former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is trying to return to Washington against Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the seat Vice President JD Vance vacated.

Late polling gives Acton a narrow edge: a polling average on Sunday put her about three points ahead, and a Research Co. survey of likely voters from October 30 to November 1 had her at 53 percent to Ramaswamy's 46, calling Ohio's races the closest it polled anywhere. The Senate race is tighter still in the same survey — Brown 49, Husted 48.

The closing days have not been quiet. Ramaswamy's campaign pulled a controversial ad featuring Acton's estranged mother after criticism that included fellow Republicans. Ohio's Senate race has drawn the second-most spending of any Senate race in the country, with Republicans outspending Democrats in October advertising, and President Trump visited Ohio three times in the final month to support Husted.

Polls close at 7:30 p.m. Tuesday. With margins this thin, Ohio's results will be among the last pieces of the national Senate puzzle to fall into place.

items.title: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame's $135 million expansion opens November 22
items.summary:
The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame's new triangular, grass-topped extension, built west of its original glass pyramid on the Cleveland lakefront, opens to the public on November 22. At $135 million, it is the museum's largest construction project since its groundbreaking in 1991, and 95 percent of the money came from local donors.

The new building is designed as the Rock Hall's public living room: mostly free to enter, starting with a lakeside garden and a new entrance with a panoramic view of Lake Erie and a full floor of giant steps. Exhibition space nearly doubles, café and food space expands, and a new two-floor events space, Baker Hall, holds up to 850 people — almost three times the previous capacity — with serious attention paid to acoustics.

Chief executive Greg Harris describes the idea simply: you come in, see the lake, and feel that music is playing. The expansion arrives a little more than three years after it was first laid out publicly in October 2023.

It is also a bright spot in a changing lakefront story — the Browns are headed to Brook Park, the port is mid-renovation, and new waterfront plans are circulating — which makes a finished, funded, opening-this-month project stand out. Worth a family trip once the doors open.

baby.tip: Day two with a newborn: start a simple log on your phone — feed times, wet diapers and dirty diapers. It feels like overkill at 3 a.m., but the pediatrician's first questions at Benji's first visit (usually a few days after discharge) are exactly those counts, and nobody remembers them on no sleep. One shared note that both Mike and Kelly can add to beats two tired memories.
baby.fact: A newborn sees best at about 8 to 12 inches — almost exactly the distance between a feeding baby's face and a parent's face. Benji's vision is still blurry and he prefers high-contrast patterns and faces, which is why face-to-face time at feeding distance is, quite literally, his favorite view in the world right now.
baby.fun: Name tidbit for the day: Benjamin is a Hebrew name meaning 'son of the right hand,' and in the Bible Benjamin was the youngest of twelve brothers — a fitting name for the newest and youngest Smiley. Today's tiny mission: tell Benji the story of his name once, out loud, even if he sleeps through the whole thing.
